summary:
AIneedHealth is a decision-support system for astronaut health self-assessment on long-duration missions, built for NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge 3/9. On distant missions, communication delay (~20 min to Mars) and no doctor on board demand medical autonomy for the crew.

It is not a vital-signs dashboard: it interprets data. Every reading is compared with the astronaut’s own baseline, set by the flight medicine team. Two analysis routes (deviation from baseline and absolute limits) classify status into 4 levels: Good, Alert, Attention, and Critical Emergency. Each alert is explainable: what happened, why, the evidence, and what to do now. The rules are referenced to NASA-STD-3001.

The prototype uses simulated wearable data, with a proposed Bluetooth architecture. It has a holographic interface with a clickable body map, a Vercel deployment, and a public repository. The 30-second pitch, narrated and captioned in English, shows the flow from data to decision.
details:
AIneedHealth is a decision-support system that helps astronauts assess their own health on long-duration missions, when communication delays of up to about 20 minutes to Mars and the absence of a doctor on board make medical autonomy essential. Instead of just displaying vital signs, it interprets them. Each reading is compared with the astronaut’s own baseline, defined by the flight medicine team. Two analysis routes run together: deviation from the personal baseline, with multi-day persistence and hysteresis to avoid false alarms, and absolute safety limits confirmed by two consecutive readings. Signals are correlated into patterns such as fatigue, dust exposure, or cardiovascular strain, and the result is one of four levels: Good, Alert, Attention, or Critical Emergency. Every alert is explainable, showing what happened, why, the evidence, and what to do now. A clickable holographic body map shows the affected region. It supports decisions and does not diagnose.

The benefit is that astronauts get a clear next step instead of raw numbers, and mission control sees the same explainable status without depending on a delayed link. The intended impact is earlier, safer decisions and less reliance on ground support as missions travel farther from Earth. The prototype was built with HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript, a Node-tested classification engine, Vercel for deployment, and GitHub for the repository. The demo video was made with Remotion, with narration generated locally by the OmniVoice engine from VoiceStudio. We used AI coding assistance during development. No hardware was used, and the prototype runs on simulated wearable data.

Our rules are referenced to NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 Rev C, the NASA Human Research Program, the CSA Bio-Monitor documentation, and a NASA Space Station blog post (March 9, 2026) describing ISS sensor data sent by Bluetooth adaptor and the goal of reducing reliance on ground support. The Bluetooth architecture is our proposal, not an operational NASA link. Our creativity lies in interpretation rather than collection: personal baselines, four-level classification, actionable explanations, and hologram-style visuals that make data readable at a glance. We prioritized safety: no diagnosis, no claim of real or real-time operational data, and sources shown wherever we state a fact. We also weighed communication delay, false alarms, and health-data privacy. Since NASA-STD-3001 sets no numeric vital-sign limits, thresholds are set per astronaut by the medical team.
